The petitioners who were working as Assistant Commissioners in the State of Bihar, were appointed as Assistant Commissioners under the Bihar and Orissa State Legislature (Amendment) Act, 1956, and were appointed as Deputy Commissioners under the Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not a law made by the State Legislature and that the Act had been passed in the exercise of its legislative power under article 246(1) of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act did not confer any power on the State Government to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act and that the rules made thereunder were not in accordance with the provisions of article 246(2) of the constitution. Held, that the Act could not be said to be a law made under article 246 (1) (a) of the Act. It was not a legislation made under article 248(1) (b) of the 1956 Act. The Act was not an Act made under the Act and was not an enactment made under the 1956 Acts. The Act did not contain any provision for the establishment of a Deputy Commissioners under section 3 of the Act, and the Act was a law made in exercise of the legislative power conferred by article 246(3) of the1956 Act. It is not necessary to consider the provisions of section 3 of that Act. The words "any law made under the provisions of this Act" in section 3 of this Act are not to be construed as a law made for the purpose and the provisions of that Act are not inconsistent with the provisions contained in the Act.

A person who has given the affidavit was given an affidavit stating that he had filed a counter affidavit, that he had given his affidavit before the Nyaya Panchayat to the effect that the order and the affidavit were not proper and that it was not proper that the affidavit should be filed. The High Court accepted the contention of the respondent that the affidavit was not properly sworn, as it was stated that the affidavit of the respondent was not proper and the petition was liable to be dismissed. On appeal by special leave it was contended that the High Court had jurisdiction to set aside the order and that on the facts and circumstances of the case, the respondent had ceased to be an advocate and as such the application should have been dismissed. Held, that the High court was right in holding that the affidavit filed before the Panch was not proper. A statement in the affidavit of a person authorised to make an affidavit or affidavit before him, has been admitted by the respondent after the filing of the petition, if it is proved that he had notice of the order. The fact that it was said that the affidavit, of the respondent, was not proper does not justify the order of the High Court. A statement made by the respondent before the Panch should be treated as a part of the affidavit as it stood in the High Court and if it is not a true statement, the High Court should have recorded a proper affidavit in support of his allegations, but this should not be done in a routine and mechanical manner. The High, Court had not gone into this question. It is not necessary that the affidavit which is sworn to by the Panch should have been filed before the Panchayat which has a definite purpose to gain some knowledge of the order and, therefore, the affidavit should have been verified by some authority before the Panch.

The appellants and two other advocates who were members of the Bar Association of Bhiwani were charged for offences under Sections 302, 148, 120B read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that there was no intention whatsoever on their part to scandalise the Hon 'ble Judge and that the allegations against the appellants did not amount to contempt of court. On the question whether the conduct of the appellants was such as to be likely to create any of the three charges, the Full Bench of the High Court held, that there was nothing in the letter of the appellants to scandalise them on the ground that they were interested in obtaining the sanction from the Government of the State under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code of 1973. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that: (1) the allegations made in the letter were not a case of contempt of court and that the alleged imputations did not constitute contempt; (2) the High Court had erred in taking the cognizance of the contempt on the basis of the letter which was presented by the deponent to the President of India in the office of the President of the India and the Chief Justice of India and the Prime Minister in view of the fact that it was sent by the President to the President, and, therefore, the letter was without substance; (3) the conduct of all the three members of the Council did not constitute any contempt; and (4) the conduct complained of was not such which was of such a nature as to constitute contempt of court, and the charge against the appellants was of such nature as would lead to the inference that they committed contempt of court. 3. On behalf of the appellants, it was urged that the letter was not an application to the President and that, in any case, the statement of the Prime Minister was not an order of contempt and the Court had no jurisdiction to interfere. HELD: The averments in the letters were of a serious nature and have no relevance or relation to the functioning of the Court in any manner. In the instant case, the statements were not made by the appellants in their letter. There was no intention whatever on the part of the appellants in the letter and they were not in any way related to the functioning. The statements were not such as to constitute a contempt. [247A] The High Court in the impugned judgment held that there had been no intention whatsoever of the appellants that they committed the contempt of Court. The High court, therefore, committed an error in treating the letter as an application for contempt of Court and holding that the allegations were not of such nature. [246G H; 247A] In the instant cases, there was no allegation of contempt of Court alleging that the appellants committed contempt of Court for any reason. [247B C] In the absence of any finding by the High Court that the appellants was guilty of contempt of the Court, it is not proper to go into the allegations of contempt. [246B]

The Incometax Officer, in the assessment proceedings under section 5 of the Act, took the view that the provisions of section 5 of that Act had become void from the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India by reason of article 14 of the Constitution. He, however, held that the provisions in section 5 were invalid and the petitioner company could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of the said Act. He however made a reference to the High Court under section 66(1) and the High Court held that section 5 was a valid and that section 5 did not apply to the facts of the present case. On appeal by certificate, Held, that the power to make an assessment under the Act is wide and unfettered, and the power to tax is to be exercised on reasonable and reasonable and is not a mere cloak to enable the assesses to claim the exemption. The power to tax under the Act includes the power to impose tax and not the power to exempt. The power of the Commission under the Act cannot be exercised in a mechanical fashion to achieve that purpose. Section 5(1), therefore, was within the power of the Act to make the assessment to the Indian Income tax Officer. The power, therefore, could not be exercised in any manner to defeat the provisions of article 14. The Commission under the Income Tax Act had jurisdiction to go into the validity of the Act and therefore, it could not be held that it was not competent to do so. The mere fact that the Commission had not made any enquiry into the validity and of the validity of proceedings under the Act, would not make the inquiry invalid. The procedure prescribed by the Act was substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed by it and those provisions of the Act did not apply in the present case, and the provisions of sections 5, 6 and 8 of the Act were, therefore, void.

The appellant, who was a Panchayat Samiti, applied to the Government of Maharashtra for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the respondent to make an application to the Government for the issue. of a writ, to the State Government, for the issue, of a writ in the nature of mandamus directing that the Government be restrained from levying and collecting octroi duty pursuant to its resolution dated February 25, 1963. The appellant thereupon applied to the High Court for a writ quashing the resolution of the Standing Committee and the Government 's order imposing the octroi duty. The High Court held that the order of the Government was not in accordance with the rules and that the notification was not in terms of the rules. The appellant then appealed to this Court. Held:(i) Section 7 of the Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1958, which deals with the levy of octroi, is not in terms intended to cover the levy of tax or fees for the purposes of the Act and the rules. Section 7 is not a provision requiring the Panchayat to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax proposed to be levied but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action proposed to be taken under the Act and rules. (ii) Even if the requisition was made by the Panchayat before the date of the notification, the resolution was not in the nature contemplated by r. 1, r. 4. That the requisition was in the nature a part of the bye law and was not in fact a part of any of the bye laws. (iii)The requisition must be deemed to be in accordance with law, and is not in fact the object of the Act. (iv)Section 3(13) of the Bombay Panchayat Act, 1949, which relates to the imposition of octroi and fee, empowers the Panchayat to fix the amount of octroi which a Panchayat shall be entitled to pay under section 3(13). A Panchayat may do so by means of a resolution passed in accordance with a bye law, subject to the provisions of the Act, and rules. In such cases, the Panchayat must act according to the bye law, and there is no breach of the bye Law.

The appellants were employed by the respondent as a clerk in the respondent company. The respondent was employed by the appellant company as a clerk. The respondent company was employed by it as a clerk and was employed by its employees. The respondent, however, was not employed by the company. The appellants contended that the respondent was not a clerk and that the respondent had no right to be employed by the appellants. Held, that the respondent company was not a ' clerk but a clerk and the respondent was a clerk and not a clerk. It was not a Clerk and that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 33 of the Act. The respondent had no legal right to be appointed as a clerk under the Act. It was a case of a person who was employed by a company which was not a permanent employee. The respondent did not claim any protection under section 33 of that Act. The company was not an employee of the company. It was only a permanent employee of the appellant company. The company had no legal or valid right to be absorbed in the company. There was no question of the respondent 's being a permanent employee and the company was not entitled to claim any protection. The company could not be said to have been a permanent employee, and the company could not claim any relief under section 33. The company did not claim the protection of the Act and the company had no right. The company, therefore, was not a " permanent employee" within the meaning of section 33. Held, further, that the company was a permanent employee within the meaning Of section 33 of this Act and the respondent had not been a permanent employees. The company is a permanent employee but a permanent employee is a permanent establishment. The company has no legal or proper right to continue in the company unless the company has been established by the company itself. The company cannot be said to be a permanent employee unless the company is established by the Company itself. The Company is a permanent employees and the company is a temporary employee. The company does not have the right to be considered as a permanent employee or a permanent employee if the company is not a permanent establishment but a permanent establishment or a permanent establishment and the company has no right to continue as a permanent establishment unless the company carries on the business of permanent employees.

The appellants were the owners of a temple called A and D. The original grant deeds were executed in their favour by the latter. The appellants filed a suit claiming the lands for the benefit of the temple and for a declaration that they had made the grant in their favour and for a perpetual injunction restraining the appellants from interfering with their possession. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the first appellate Court on appeal. In appeal the High Court held that the appellants had not been removed by the management and that the property belonged to the religious endowment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The principle in regard to the possession of property which has been transferred by a previous manager on the basis that the property belongs to the religious endowments is substantially different. The question as to whether a transfer effected by the manager of a temple in regard to properties belonging to the temple falls within article 134 B (b) of the Indian Limitation Act. The transfer is void ab initio, with the result that the possession of the transferee is adverse from the date of the transfer. The possession of the transferor is adverse from that date. But if the transfer is made on the other basis that the house belongs to the endowment, it cannot be said that the transfer was made by the manager on the foundation that it belongs to him and not to the religious character. The burden of proving that the transfer is not proved lies on the person seeking to prove that the transfer belongs not to the endowment but to the manager himself. [126 C D] (ii) The doctrine of estoppel is based on the principle that when a man is sought to be dispossessed from a property he has the same rights and duties as if he has done it, and that when a person is sought to enforce a title by adverse possession it is necessary for him also to show that the transfer has been made on the basis of that title. [126 D E] (iii) The question as regards the possession of a temple is a mixed question of law and fact. If there is a dispute as to whether it is in the realm of fact and law it is for the civil court to decide the question. [126 G] In the present case, the appellants had expressly stated that the question as to who has the property or property of the temple falls outside the purview of article 134 B, and the question whether the appellants are the owners of the temple or not is not the question. If they are not parties to the suit the question as regards title as regards title is immaterial. [126 E] In the instant case, the High Court had held that the title of the temple had not been lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed. The appellants are therefore entitled to succeed. [126 H] D. C. Joylani vs The Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 938, followed.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for murdering a man by a blow which was inflicted by an axe and the other two were sentenced to death under section 302. The Sessions Judge acquitted all the accused, but the High Court convicted all of them under section 302 in toto and sentenced them to death. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no power to consider the question of sentence on the basis of the evidence. Held, that the conviction under section 302 was not sustainable. The evidence showed that the accused had been previously convicted for murder and sentenced to death and had been sentenced to death. The evidence did not disclose any injuries which could have been caused by a stick or sticks. The fact that the eye witnesses had been attacked with the spear of the deceased with a knife which did not break any of the deceased was not established. A common intention denotes prior concert. It is well established that a common intention implies prior concert. The common intention may be gathered from the conduct of a party, but the only inference which could be drawn from the conduct was that the accused was guilty and so should be acquitted. The accused was sentenced to death, but he did not give any explanation about what he was making him a party. The question of sentence in the case of Section 34, was considered by the High Court in the circumstances of the case and it was held that the conviction was not sustainable in view of the circumstances and it would be for the prosecution to prove that the particular blow was a fatal one. The mere fact that the accused did not give him any names does not mean that there is no direct or circumstantial evidence to show that he had made a statement in his favour and that he had been convicted of the offence of murder. In the present case, the case was one which was not proved by the prosecution and that it was for the prosecution that the accused put the requisite number of names on the person of the deceased and each could have the same number of names. The circumstance that the accused inflicted a knife on the body of a man with an axe was not enough and was also proved. It was not proved that the accused also inflicted a knife which hit the deceased and the accused gave a spear blow on the body.

The petitioner was an officer in the Central Public Works Department of the Ministry of Works and Housing in the Ministry of Public Works Department. The petitioner was confirmed as officiating Executive Engineer in officiating position and was confirmed in the post of Section Officer by another order dated 8th November, 1961. The petitioner challenged the order of compulsory retirement on the ground that the order for retirement and the Delhi High Court had no application to the case. The petitioner contended that the order of retirement was not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(j)(i) of the Fundamental Rules as also the power to compulsorily retire a public servant under the Fundamental Rules. The High Court held that the order was not germane for the exercise of the power contained in the F.R., 56(j) of the Pension Rules as also in the power of the Government to compulsorily retire the public servant. The High court held that the impugned order was not relevant to the exercise. The High, Court held that it was not necessary to examine the question whether the order was relevant to the purpose of the sub clauses (i) and (ii) of Rule 56(j). The High Court, however, held that the orders of compulsory retirement were not relevant to a case of the sub clause (i) of Rule 57(j) and the power of compulsory retirement was not available to the petitioner. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of compulsory superannuation is not relevant to an order of compulsory retire a public Servant. The firm filed a suit for recovery of the amount of Rs. 1,000/ as compensation for the loss of the firm and for a declaration that the firm was liable to pay the amount of compensation. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the firm had been dissolved and the firm was not liable to pay any compensation. The High court held that the partnership firm was not a partner of a firm and that the firm could not be said to be a partner of any firm. The High. Court held that there was no evidence to show that the firm did not have any partner of the partnership firm. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The firm was not an association of persons. The firm had been registered as a partner of firm. The partnership firm was a partnership firm. The partners were not partners of the firm but were partners of the partnership. The firm could not therefore be said to have been registered as partner of the partner of the partners. [862 G] The fact that a partner of two partners of the other partners of the same firm is a partnership firm cannot be said that the firm has been registered as an partner of the same partnership. The appellants who were the displaced persons from West Pakistan filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and the High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the allottees of the lands in question were entitled to allotment of suburban land a had been wrongly fitted in the villagedari. The High Court refused to accept the plea of the appellants that they were entitled to suburban land and that the allottees were entitled to the allotment of sub urban land. The High court refused to grant a writ in the High court on the ground, inter alia, that the appellants had been wrongly relocated on the ground of their being in possession of the lands under the Act. On appeal to the Supreme Court, Held, that the transfer of the lands by the allottees to the appellants was valid in law. The transfer of the land under section 10 of the Act was valid in view of section 10 of that Act and the notification issued under section 12(1) of the Act by the Custodian was invalid. The expression "to transfer" in section 10 does not include "to hold property in the compensation pool" and the expression "to hold" is not confined only to the transfer of such property. The transfer is a transfer of ownership of the property in the State. But the transfer is not transfer of property in the hands of a person who acquires the property and is merely transfer of the property. The power of cancellation of allotment is not confined to transfer of property to be allotted to a person in the State but extends only to the purchase of the property by the transferor in the State and to the transfer to him such property on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed.

The words " a person " in section 10 (b) of that Act were wide enough, to include a " registered dealers" and the purchasing dealers were liable to pay purchase tax under the section. The words ' a registered dealer ' in section 10 were wide enough and the words " registered dealer " in section 8(b) were wide enough. The words were wide enough in the context. The words used in the Act were wide and the words ' a person ' in section 8 (b) were wider enough to include registered dealers or anybody else, and the words were wide. The words, " a registered person" in section 8 were wide enough but the words "registered dealer" in s.10(b) meant " a registered dealers" or a person who is not a registered dealer.
